Physiology-03.question: ১) A raised blood pH & Bicarbonate level is consistent with-?
Physiology-03.option2: Chronic renal failure with raised PC02
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is persistent vomiting of gastric content. Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) through prolonged vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis, characterized by:

  • ↑ Blood pH (alkalaemia)

  • ↑ Serum bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Chronic renal failure with raised PCO₂ – Causes metabolic acidosis (↓ bicarbonate); respiratory compensation may increase PCO₂ but pH is usually low.

  • Partly compensated respiratory alkalosis – Primary change is ↓ PCO₂; bicarbonate is usually decreased due to renal compensation.

  • Metabolic acidosis – Causes ↓ pH and ↓ bicarbonate.

High-yield points:

ABG patterns:

Disorder pH HCO₃⁻ PCO₂
Metabolic alkalosis (vomiting) ↑ ↑ ↑ (compensation)
Metabolic acidosis ↓ ↓ ↓ (compensation)
Respiratory alkalosis ↑ ↓ ↓
Respiratory acidosis ↓ ↑ ↑

Exam pearl:
↑ pH + ↑ bicarbonate = Metabolic alkalosis → vomiting of gastric contents.

Physiology-03.question: ২) Primary function of the basal ganglia is-?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is planning of voluntary movement. The basal ganglia play a major role in the initiation, planning, coordination, and regulation of voluntary movements by modulating motor pathways through the thalamus and cerebral cortex.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Short-term memory – Mainly associated with the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus.

  • Neuroendocrine control – Controlled primarily by the hypothalamus and pituitary gland.

  • Slow wave sleep – Associated mainly with the hypothalamus, brainstem, and thalamic networks.

High-yield points:

Basal ganglia functions:

  • Initiation and smooth execution of voluntary movement

  • Regulation of muscle tone

  • Suppression of unwanted movements

Clinical correlation:

  • Parkinson disease → ↓ dopamine in substantia nigra → bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor

  • Huntington disease → degeneration of caudate nucleus → chorea

Exam pearl:
Basal ganglia = planning and modulation of voluntary movement.

Physiology-03.question: ৩) Most widely distributed excitatory neurotransmitter -?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is glutamate. Glutamate is the most widely distributed excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system (CNS) and is responsible for fast excitatory synaptic transmission.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Acetylcholine – Important neurotransmitter at neuromuscular junction, autonomic nervous system, and memory pathways, but not the most widely distributed excitatory neurotransmitter.

  • Glycine – Mainly an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem.

  • Dopamine – A modulatory neurotransmitter involved in movement, reward, and endocrine regulation.

High-yield points:

Major CNS neurotransmitters:

Neurotransmitter Main role
Glutamate Most common excitatory neurotransmitter
GABA Most common inhibitory neurotransmitter in brain
Glycine Inhibitory neurotransmitter (spinal cord)
Dopamine Movement, reward, endocrine control
Acetylcholine NMJ, memory, autonomic functions

Exam pearl:
Most widely distributed excitatory neurotransmitter = Glutamate.

Physiology-03.question: ৪) Upper motor neuron inhibits Lower motor neuron by releasing-?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is glycine. Upper motor neurons (UMN) influence lower motor neurons (LMN) through inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord, which release glycine, producing inhibition of LMN activity.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Glutamate – Major excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS.

  • Aspartate – An excitatory amino acid neurotransmitter.

  • Acetylcholine – Released by LMN at the neuromuscular junction to stimulate skeletal muscle contraction.

High-yield points:

Neurotransmitters:

Neurotransmitter Function
Glycine Inhibitory neurotransmitter in spinal cord
GABA Main inhibitory neurotransmitter in brain
Glutamate Main excitatory neurotransmitter
Acetylcholine NMJ transmission

Exam pearl:
UMN inhibition of LMN → Glycine (spinal inhibitory neurotransmitter).

Physiology-03.question: ৫) Which lens is used in myopia?
৬) Lesion of left optic radiation results in
৭) Inability to recognize or detect any odor
৮) Merkel disc is concerned with
৯) Which one is concerned with converting recent memory to long term memory?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is hippocampus. The hippocampus is responsible for the consolidation of recent memory into long-term memory. It converts short-term memories into more permanent storage in the cerebral cortex.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Amygdala – Involved in emotional processing and fear memory.

  • Putamen – Part of the basal ganglia; involved in motor control and procedural learning.

  • Pallidum (globus pallidus) – Part of basal ganglia; regulates movement and muscle tone.

High-yield points:

Memory-related structures:

Structure Function
Hippocampus Short-term → long-term memory consolidation
Amygdala Emotional memory
Cerebral cortex Long-term memory storage
Basal ganglia Procedural/motor learning

Exam pearl:
Conversion of recent memory to long-term memory = Hippocampus.

Physiology-03.question: ১০) Post ganglionic neurotransmitter of sympathetic division
১১) Tract carries pain and temperature from opposite side
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is spinothalamic tract. The spinothalamic tract (anterolateral system) carries pain, temperature, and crude touch sensations from the opposite (contralateral) side of the body to the brain.

The fibres cross to the opposite side in the spinal cord through the anterior white commissure shortly after entering.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Dorsal column – Carries fine touch, vibration, and proprioception; fibres cross in the medulla.

  • Corticospinal tract – Carries voluntary motor signals.

  • Geniculocalcarine tract – Carries visual information from the lateral geniculate body to the visual cortex.

High-yield points:

Tract Function Crossing
Spinothalamic tract Pain & temperature Spinal cord
Dorsal column Fine touch, vibration, proprioception Medulla
Corticospinal tract Motor function Medulla (pyramidal decussation)

Exam pearl:
Pain + temperature from opposite side = Spinothalamic tract.

Physiology-03.question: ১২) Most important characteristic of synaptic transmission-
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is one-way conduction. The most important characteristic of synaptic transmission is that it is unidirectional because neurotransmitter is released only from the presynaptic terminal and receptors are present on the postsynaptic membrane.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Excitation – Synapses may be excitatory or inhibitory; excitation is not the defining feature.

  • Synaptic delay – A characteristic feature of chemical synapses, but not the most important.

  • Summation – Occurs in neurons when multiple postsynaptic potentials combine, but it is not the primary characteristic.

High-yield points:

Characteristics of chemical synaptic transmission:

  • One-way conduction (unidirectional)

  • Synaptic delay (~0.5 ms)

  • Fatigability

  • Summation

  • Facilitation and inhibition

Exam pearl:
Most important characteristic of synapse = One-way conduction.

Physiology-03.question: ১৩) Nerve fiber for slow pain
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Type C nerve fibres. Slow pain (second pain) is transmitted by unmyelinated, small-diameter C fibres, producing a dull, aching, burning sensation that is poorly localized.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Aδ fibres – Carry fast pain (first pain), which is sharp, pricking, and well localized.

  • Aβ fibres – Carry touch, pressure, and vibration sensations.

  • Aα fibres – Carry proprioception and motor signals.

High-yield points:

Fibre type Function Speed
Aδ Fast, sharp pain Fast
C fibre Slow, dull pain Slow
Aβ Touch, vibration Fast
Aα Motor, proprioception Fastest

Exam pearl:
Slow pain = C fibre; Fast pain = Aδ fibre.

Physiology-03.question: ১৪) Which of the following substances or combinations of substances could be used to measure interstitial fluid volume?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is mannitol. To measure interstitial fluid volume, a substance must distribute throughout the extracellular fluid (ECF) but not enter cells and not remain confined to plasma.

Mannitol distributes in the extracellular space and can be used to estimate ECF volume. By subtracting plasma volume from ECF volume:

Interstitial fluid volume = Extracellular fluid volume − Plasma volume

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Evans blue – Binds to albumin and remains within the plasma, so it measures plasma volume.

  • Inulin and D₂O –

    • Inulin → measures ECF volume

    • D₂O (deuterium oxide) → measures total body water
      Not used alone to directly measure interstitial fluid volume.

  • Inulin and radioactive albumin –

    • Inulin → ECF volume

    • Radioactive albumin → plasma volume
      Their difference can calculate interstitial fluid volume, but not a direct single substance measurement.

High-yield points:

Fluid compartment Marker
Total body water D₂O, tritiated water
Extracellular fluid Inulin, mannitol
Plasma volume Evans blue, radioactive albumin
Interstitial fluid ECF − Plasma volume

Exam pearl:
Mannitol → ECF marker → used for estimating interstitial fluid volume.

Physiology-03.question: ১৫) Erythropoietin is secreted by-?
Physiology-03.option3: granular cells in the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
Physiology-03.option4: Cells in the peritubular capillary bed.
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is cells in the peritubular capillary bed. Erythropoietin (EPO) is produced mainly by peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells in the renal cortex. It is released in response to renal hypoxia and stimulates the bone marrow to increase red blood cell production.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Cells in the proximal tubules – Responsible for reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, and electrolytes; not EPO secretion.

  • Cells in the distal tubules – Involved in electrolyte regulation and acid–base balance.

  • Granular cells in the juxtaglomerular apparatus – Secrete renin, not erythropoietin.

High-yield points:

Renal cell Hormone/function
Peritubular interstitial cells Erythropoietin secretion
Juxtaglomerular granular cells Renin secretion
Distal tubule Na⁺/K⁺ regulation, acid–base control
Proximal tubule Major reabsorption site

Exam pearl:
Kidney hypoxia → peritubular interstitial cells → EPO → ↑ RBC production.

Physiology-03.question: ১৬) Dehydration increases the plasma concentration of all the following hormones except -?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP). During dehydration, plasma volume decreases, causing reduced atrial stretch. This leads to decreased secretion of ANP.

The other hormones increase during dehydration to conserve water and maintain blood pressure:

  • Vasopressin (ADH) ↑ – Released due to increased plasma osmolality and reduced blood volume; increases water reabsorption in kidneys.

  • Angiotensin II ↑ – Activates the renin–angiotensin system due to reduced renal perfusion; causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone secretion.

  • Norepinephrine ↑ – Increased sympathetic activity causes vasoconstriction and helps maintain blood pressure.

High-yield points:

Dehydration response:

Hormone Change
Vasopressin (ADH) ↑
Angiotensin II ↑
Norepinephrine ↑
Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) ↓

Exam pearl:
Dehydration → low atrial stretch → ↓ ANP.

Physiology-03.question: ১৭) In absence of vasopressin, the greatest fraction of filtered water is reabsorbed in the-?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is PCT. Even in the absence of vasopressin (ADH), the greatest fraction of filtered water (~65%) is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule through obligatory water reabsorption coupled with sodium and solute reabsorption.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • DCT (Distal convoluted tubule) – Reabsorbs only a small amount of water; water permeability is mainly regulated by ADH.

  • ALLH (Ascending limb of loop of Henle) – Impermeable to water; does not reabsorb water.

  • DLLH (Descending limb of loop of Henle) – Permeable to water and contributes to water reabsorption, but less than the PCT.

High-yield points:

Water reabsorption along nephron:

Site Approximate water reabsorption
PCT ~65% (ADH independent)
Descending limb of loop of Henle ~15%
DCT Small amount (ADH dependent)
Collecting duct Variable, ADH dependent

Exam pearl:
No ADH → maximum water reabsorption still occurs in PCT.

Physiology-03.question: ১৮) Renin also known as angiotensinogenase is circulating enzyme released mainly by JG cells in the juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidneys plasma renin levels are decreased in patients with-?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is primary hyperaldosteronism. In primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), excess aldosterone causes sodium and water retention, increasing blood volume and suppressing renin release through negative feedback. Therefore:

  • ↑ Aldosterone

  • ↓ Renin

  • ↓ Plasma renin activity

The other options are incorrect because they stimulate renin release:

  • Renal artery stenosis – Reduced renal perfusion stimulates JG cells → ↑ renin.

  • Salt restriction – Decreased sodium delivery/volume stimulates RAAS → ↑ renin.

  • Upright posture – Reduced renal perfusion and increased sympathetic activity stimulate ↑ renin.

High-yield points:

Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS):

Condition Renin Aldosterone
Primary hyperaldosteronism ↓ ↑
Secondary hyperaldosteronism (renal artery stenosis) ↑ ↑
Salt restriction ↑ ↑
Dehydration ↑ ↑

Exam pearl:
High aldosterone + low renin = Primary hyperaldosteronism.

Physiology-03.question: ১৯) Neurotransmitter of Fast pain-
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is glutamate. Fast pain (first pain) is transmitted mainly by Aδ fibres, and the neurotransmitter released at the first synapse in the dorsal horn is glutamate.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Substance P – Mainly involved in transmission of slow, dull, burning pain through C fibres.

  • Serotonin – A modulatory neurotransmitter involved in mood and other CNS functions.

  • Acetylcholine – Used at neuromuscular junction and autonomic synapses, not the main pain neurotransmitter.

High-yield points:

Pain type Fibre Neurotransmitter
Fast pain Aδ fibre Glutamate
Slow pain C fibre Substance P + glutamate

Exam pearl:
Fast sharp pain → Aδ fibre → Glutamate
Slow burning pain → C fibre → Substance P.

Physiology-03.question: ২০) Which nucleus of hypothalamus controls circadian rhythm?
২১) Which of the following substances has the highest renal clearance?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is para-aminohippuric acid (PAH). PAH has the highest renal clearance because it is:

  • Freely filtered at the glomerulus

  • Actively secreted by proximal tubules

  • Almost completely removed from plasma in a single pass through the kidney

Therefore, PAH clearance is used to estimate renal plasma flow (RPF).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Inulin – Freely filtered but not reabsorbed or secreted; used to measure GFR, but clearance is lower than PAH.

  • Glucose – Freely filtered but normally completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule → clearance ≈ 0.

  • Na⁺ – Freely filtered but extensively reabsorbed → low clearance.

High-yield points:

Substance Renal handling Use
PAH Filtered + secreted → almost complete removal Renal plasma flow
Inulin Filtered only GFR measurement
Creatinine Filtered + slight secretion Clinical GFR estimation
Glucose Filtered + reabsorbed Clearance ≈ 0

Exam pearl:
Highest renal clearance = PAH (≈ effective renal plasma flow).

Physiology-03.question: ২২) Which of the following is a cause of metabolic alkalosis?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is hyperaldosteronism. Excess aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron and promotes potassium and hydrogen ion secretion, causing:

  • ↑ H⁺ loss

  • ↑ HCO₃⁻ retention

  • Metabolic alkalosis

The other options are incorrect because they cause metabolic acidosis:

  • Chronic renal failure – Reduced acid excretion → accumulation of acids → metabolic acidosis.

  • Ethylene glycol ingestion – Causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to toxic metabolites (glycolic acid and oxalic acid).

  • Treatment with acetazolamide – Carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes bicarbonate loss in urine → metabolic acidosis.

High-yield points:

Causes of metabolic alkalosis:

  • Vomiting / gastric acid loss

  • Diuretics (loop, thiazide)

  • Hyperaldosteronism

  • Excess alkali intake

Causes of metabolic acidosis:

  • Renal failure

  • Diabetic ketoacidosis

  • Lactic acidosis

  • Ethylene glycol poisoning

  • Acetazolamide

Exam pearl:
Aldosterone excess → ↑ H⁺ secretion → metabolic alkalosis.

Physiology-03.question: ২৩) Feature of UMNL
২৪) Deep sensation
২৫) Presbycusis is –
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is age-related hearing impairment. Presbycusis is a progressive sensorineural hearing loss due to ageing, mainly affecting the high-frequency sounds because of degeneration of cochlear hair cells and auditory pathways.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Age related vision impairment – Called presbyopia (loss of near vision due to reduced lens elasticity).

  • Age related balance impairment – Related to vestibular system degeneration, not presbycusis.

  • Age related memory impairment – Related to cognitive ageing or neurodegenerative disorders.

High-yield points:

Term Meaning
Presbycusis Age-related sensorineural hearing loss
Presbyopia Age-related loss of near vision
Presbyphagia Age-related swallowing difficulty

Exam pearl:
Presbycusis = elderly patient + bilateral high-frequency hearing loss.

Physiology-03.question: ২৬) In the pain pathway-?
Physiology-03.option1: The principal receptor is the Meissner's corpuscle
Physiology-03.option2: The first order neuron is the pain receptor
Physiology-03.option3: The third order neuron projects from the thalamus
Physiology-03.option4: Perception occurs in the secondary cortex
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is the third-order neuron projects from the thalamus. In the pain pathway:

  1. First-order neuron – Begins from pain receptors (free nerve endings) in peripheral tissues and enters the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.

  2. Second-order neuron – Crosses in the spinal cord and ascends through the spinothalamic tract to the thalamus.

  3. Third-order neuron – Arises from the thalamus and projects to the primary somatosensory cortex for conscious perception of pain.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • The principal receptor is Meissner's corpuscle – Incorrect. Meissner corpuscles detect light touch, not pain. Pain receptors are free nerve endings (nociceptors).

  • The first-order neuron is the pain receptor – Incorrect. The first-order neuron is the sensory neuron, not the receptor itself.

  • Perception occurs in the secondary cortex – Incorrect. Pain perception occurs mainly in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), with secondary areas involved in processing.

High-yield points:

Pain pathway:

Free nerve ending → 1st order neuron → spinal cord → spinothalamic tract → thalamus → 3rd order neuron → primary somatosensory cortex

Exam pearl:
Pain receptor = free nerve ending; 3rd-order neuron originates from thalamus.

Physiology-03.question: ২৭) Medial geniculate body is concerned with -
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is audition (hearing). The medial geniculate body (MGB) of the thalamus acts as the relay station for auditory information from the inferior colliculus to the primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Vision – Relayed by the lateral geniculate body (LGB).

  • Olfaction – Does not have a primary thalamic relay in the classic pathway.

  • Gustation (taste) – Relayed through the ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus.

High-yield points:

Thalamic nucleus Function
Medial geniculate body Audition (hearing)
Lateral geniculate body Vision
VPL nucleus Body sensation
VPM nucleus Face sensation and taste

Exam pearl:
Medial geniculate = Music (hearing); Lateral geniculate = Light (vision).

Physiology-03.question: ২৮) Corticospinal tract lesion leads to
Physiology-03.option4: Weakness of distal group of muscles of hands and feet
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is exaggerated knee jerk. A lesion of the corticospinal tract (upper motor neuron lesion) causes loss of descending inhibitory control over spinal reflex arcs, resulting in:

  • Hyperreflexia (exaggerated deep tendon reflexes)

  • Increased muscle tone (spasticity)

  • Positive Babinski sign

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Loss of all tendon reflexes – Occurs in lower motor neuron lesions due to damage to the reflex arc.

  • Decreased muscle tone – UMN lesions cause increased muscle tone (spasticity).

  • Weakness of distal group of muscles of hands and feet – Distal weakness can occur in UMN lesions, but it is not the characteristic finding tested here.

High-yield points:

UMN lesion features:

  • Spastic paralysis

  • ↑ Muscle tone

  • ↑ Deep tendon reflexes

  • Clonus

  • Extensor plantar response (Babinski sign)

LMN lesion features:

  • Flaccid paralysis

  • ↓ Muscle tone

  • ↓/absent reflexes

  • Fasciculations

  • Muscle wasting

Exam pearl:
Corticospinal tract lesion → exaggerated reflexes (hyperreflexia).

Physiology-03.question: ২৯) The light reflex involves the following structure –
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Edinger–Westphal nucleus. The pupillary light reflex involves:

Retina → Optic nerve (CN II) → Optic tract → Pretectal nucleus → Edinger–Westphal nucleus → Oculomotor nerve (CN III) → Ciliary ganglion → Sphincter pupillae → Pupil constriction

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Sublingual ganglion – Not involved in pupillary reflex; associated with salivary gland innervation.

  • Lateral geniculate body – Relay centre for vision to the visual cortex, not the light reflex pathway.

  • Vestibular nerve – Involved in balance and vestibular function.

High-yield points:

Pupillary light reflex:

  • Afferent limb → CN II (optic nerve)

  • Centre → Pretectal nucleus

  • Efferent limb → CN III (oculomotor nerve)

  • Parasympathetic nucleus → Edinger–Westphal nucleus

Exam pearl:
Light reflex → Edinger–Westphal nucleus → CN III → pupil constriction.

Physiology-03.question: ৩০) Root value of knee jerk
৩১) Inhibitory neurotransmitter
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid). GABA is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system (CNS), especially in the brain. It reduces neuronal excitability by increasing chloride influx (GABA-A receptor) or increasing potassium efflux (GABA-B receptor).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Acetylcholine – Mainly an excitatory neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction and involved in autonomic functions.

  • Histamine – Functions mainly in wakefulness, gastric secretion, and immune responses; not a major inhibitory neurotransmitter.

  • Nitric oxide (NO) – A neuromodulator involved in vasodilation and synaptic signalling, not the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter.

High-yield points:

Physiology-03.question: ৩২) Hormones secreted by kidneys excludes
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is noradrenalin. The kidney secretes several important hormones and hormone-like substances, but noradrenaline is not a renal hormone; it is mainly released from sympathetic nerve endings and the adrenal medulla.

The other options are associated with renal secretion:

  • Erythropoietin – Produced by peritubular interstitial cells of the renal cortex; stimulates RBC production.

  • Thrombopoietin – Produced mainly by the liver, but the kidney also contributes to its production.

  • Prostaglandins – Synthesized in the kidney and involved in regulation of renal blood flow and sodium handling.

High-yield points:

Renal hormones/substances:

  • Renin → juxtaglomerular cells

  • Erythropoietin → peritubular interstitial cells

  • Prostaglandins → renal synthesis

  • Calcitriol (active vitamin D) → kidney activation

Exam pearl:
Noradrenaline = sympathetic neurotransmitter, not a kidney hormone.

Physiology-03.question: ৩৩) Highest capacity of reabsorption
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is PCT. The proximal convoluted tubule has the highest capacity for reabsorption in the nephron and reabsorbs approximately:

  • 65–70% of filtered Na⁺ and water

  • Nearly 100% of glucose and amino acids (under normal conditions)

  • Most bicarbonate, phosphate, and other solutes

The other options are incorrect because:

  • DCT (Distal convoluted tubule) – Responsible mainly for fine regulation of electrolytes; reabsorbs a smaller fraction.

  • LOH (Loop of Henle) – Important for establishing the medullary concentration gradient but has less total reabsorptive capacity.

  • CD (Collecting duct) – Regulates final water balance under ADH control.

High-yield points:

Nephron segment Main function
PCT Maximum reabsorption
Loop of Henle Counter-current mechanism
DCT Fine electrolyte adjustment
Collecting duct ADH-dependent water reabsorption

Exam pearl:
Greatest reabsorptive capacity of nephron = PCT.

Physiology-03.question: ৩৪) The glomerular capillaries cannot filtrate...?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is plasma protein. The glomerular filtration barrier allows filtration of small molecules such as glucose, sodium, and creatinine but normally prevents the passage of large plasma proteins (especially albumin).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Glucose – Freely filtered at the glomerulus and normally completely reabsorbed in the PCT.

  • Sodium – Freely filtered and later reabsorbed throughout the nephron.

  • Creatinine – Freely filtered (with a small amount of tubular secretion) and used clinically to estimate GFR.

High-yield points:

Glomerular filtration barrier:

  1. Fenestrated endothelium

  2. Glomerular basement membrane

  3. Podocyte slit diaphragm

Normally filtered:

  • Water

  • Electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻)

  • Glucose

  • Urea

  • Creatinine

Not filtered:

  • Large plasma proteins (albumin)

  • Blood cells

Exam pearl:
Glomerulus filters small solutes but retains plasma proteins and cells.

Physiology-03.question: ৩৫) Renal autoregulation is important to maintain the
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is GFR (glomerular filtration rate). Renal autoregulation maintains a relatively constant GFR despite changes in systemic blood pressure (approximately between 80–180 mmHg).

It occurs mainly through:

  • Myogenic mechanism – Afferent arteriole constriction/dilation in response to pressure changes.

  • Tubuloglomerular feedback – Macula densa regulates afferent arteriolar tone.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • RPF (renal plasma flow) – Not the primary parameter maintained by autoregulation.

  • BP (blood pressure) – Controlled mainly by systemic cardiovascular and hormonal mechanisms, not renal autoregulation.

  • Osmolarity – Regulated mainly by ADH, thirst mechanism, and renal concentrating ability.

High-yield points:

Renal autoregulation maintains:

  • GFR

  • Renal blood flow (to some extent)

Mechanisms:

  1. Myogenic response

  2. Tubuloglomerular feedback

Exam pearl:
Renal autoregulation → keeps GFR constant despite BP fluctuations.

Physiology-03.question: ৩৬) Presence of positive benedict's test indicate that there might be a problem in
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is PCT. A positive Benedict's test indicates the presence of reducing sugars (mainly glucose) in urine. Normally, glucose is freely filtered at the glomerulus and completely reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.

Therefore, a problem in the PCT (or saturation of glucose transporters in diabetes mellitus) can lead to glucosuria and a positive Benedict's test.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • DCT (Distal convoluted tubule) – Mainly involved in electrolyte regulation, not glucose reabsorption.

  • LOH (Loop of Henle) – Responsible for concentration of urine; does not normally reabsorb glucose.

  • CD (Collecting duct) – Regulates water balance through ADH; not involved in glucose handling.

High-yield points:

Glucose handling in kidney:

  • Filtration → Glomerulus

  • Reabsorption → PCT (Na⁺-glucose cotransporter)

  • Excretion → When transport maximum (Tm) is exceeded → glucosuria

Exam pearl:
Positive Benedict's test → urinary glucose → PCT dysfunction or diabetes mellitus.

Physiology-03.question: ৩৭) Limiting pH of urine
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is 4.5. The minimum (limiting) pH of urine is approximately 4.5, meaning the kidney cannot acidify urine below this level under normal physiological conditions.

The kidney maintains urine pH usually between 4.5–8.0 depending on acid–base status.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 3.5 – Below the physiological minimum urine pH.

  • 4 – Lower than the normal limiting value.

  • 5 – Within the acidic urine range but not the minimum.

High-yield points:

Urine pH:

  • Normal range → 4.5–8.0

  • Minimum (most acidic) → 4.5

  • Maximum (most alkaline) → 8.0

Exam pearl:
Limiting pH of urine = 4.5.

Physiology-03.question: ৩৮) Normal GFR is .... L/day?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is 180 L/day. The normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is approximately:

  • 125 mL/min

  • ≈ 180 L/day

This represents the amount of plasma filtered by the glomeruli per day.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 125 L/day – Represents GFR in mL/min (125 mL/min), not daily volume.

  • 625 L/day – Too high; not physiological.

  • 290 L/day – Higher than normal filtration volume.

High-yield points:

GFR calculation:

125 mL/min×60×24≈180,000 mL/day125 mL/min×60×24≈180,000 mL/day

= 180 L/day

Exam pearl:
Normal GFR = 125 mL/min ≈ 180 L/day.

Physiology-03.question: ৩৯) Kidney synthesize glucose by the process of
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is gluconeogenesis. The kidney can synthesize glucose by producing glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors such as lactate, glycerol, and amino acids through the process of gluconeogenesis, especially during prolonged fasting.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Glycolysis – Breakdown of glucose to produce energy; does not synthesize glucose.

  • Glycogenesis – Formation of glycogen from glucose for storage.

  • Glucogenesis – Not a standard physiological term (often confused with gluconeogenesis).

High-yield points:

Renal glucose metabolism:

  • Kidney cortex performs gluconeogenesis

  • Becomes important during:

    • Prolonged fasting

    • Starvation

    • Metabolic acidosis

Exam pearl:
Liver + kidney = major organs for gluconeogenesis.

Physiology-03.question: ৪০) About what % of human body is fluid?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is 60%. In an average adult, total body water (TBW) accounts for approximately 60% of body weight.

The distribution is:

  • Intracellular fluid (ICF) → ~40% of body weight (2/3 of TBW)

  • Extracellular fluid (ECF) → ~20% of body weight (1/3 of TBW)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 40% – Represents approximately the intracellular fluid compartment, not total body fluid.

  • 50% – Approximate body water in some elderly individuals or those with higher body fat.

  • 65% – Closer to infants or lean individuals but not the average adult.

High-yield points:

Body fluid distribution:

Compartment % of body weight
Total body water ~60%
Intracellular fluid ~40%
Extracellular fluid ~20%

Exam pearl:

Physiology-03.question: ৪১) Regarding basal ganglia-
Physiology-03.option1: It is a part of pyramidal system
Physiology-03.option2: It is associated with temperature regulation
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is its lesion produces Huntington disease. The basal ganglia are involved in the regulation of voluntary movement. Degeneration of the caudate nucleus and putamen (striatum) causes Huntington disease, characterized by choreiform movements and psychiatric symptoms.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • It is a part of pyramidal system – Incorrect. Basal ganglia are part of the extrapyramidal system, not the pyramidal system.

  • It is associated with temperature regulation – Incorrect. Temperature regulation is mainly controlled by the hypothalamus.

  • It controls posture and equilibrium – Incorrect. Posture and balance are mainly controlled by the cerebellum and vestibular system.

High-yield points:

Basal ganglia functions:

  • Initiation and regulation of voluntary movement

  • Suppression of unwanted movements

  • Regulation of muscle tone

Clinical correlations:

  • Parkinson disease → Substantia nigra degeneration → ↓ dopamine → bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor

  • Huntington disease → Caudate nucleus degeneration → chorea

Exam pearl:
Basal ganglia lesion → Huntington disease (caudate degeneration).

Physiology-03.question: ৪২) Which of the following areas is predominantly concerned with thermoregulation?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is hypothalamus. The hypothalamus is the main centre for thermoregulation and maintains body temperature by coordinating heat production and heat loss mechanisms.

  • Anterior hypothalamus → Responsible mainly for heat loss (sweating, vasodilation).

  • Posterior hypothalamus → Responsible mainly for heat conservation and heat production (shivering, vasoconstriction).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Anterior pituitary – Controls endocrine functions through hormone secretion, not temperature regulation.

  • Cerebellum – Coordinates movement, posture, and balance.

  • Brain stem – Involved in vital functions such as respiration and cardiovascular control, but not the primary thermoregulatory centre.

High-yield points:

Area Main function
Hypothalamus Thermoregulation
Anterior hypothalamus Heat loss
Posterior hypothalamus Heat conservation
Cerebellum Coordination & balance

Exam pearl:
Body temperature control centre = Hypothalamus.

Physiology-03.question: ৪৩) Net filtration pressure in glomerulus (mmHg)
৪৪) Clearance rate is minimum for
৪৫) Contraindications of Lumber puncture-?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is papilledema. Papilledema indicates raised intracranial pressure (ICP), and performing a lumbar puncture in this situation can cause brain herniation due to sudden reduction of CSF pressure.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Septicemia – Not an absolute contraindication; LP may be performed if meningitis is suspected (with appropriate assessment).

  • Elderly patient – Age alone is not a contraindication.

  • Spinal deformity – May make the procedure technically difficult but is not the most important contraindication.

High-yield points:

Contraindications of lumbar puncture:

  • Raised intracranial pressure (e.g., papilledema, mass lesion)

  • Infection at the puncture site

  • Significant bleeding disorder / severe thrombocytopenia

  • Severe spinal abnormalities (relative)

Exam pearl:
Papilledema → suspect raised ICP → avoid lumbar puncture.

Physiology-03.question: ৪৬) Following Which is a Bipolar Neuron-?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is vestibular ganglia. Bipolar neurons have one axon and one dendrite extending from opposite poles of the cell body. They are found mainly in special sensory pathways, including:

  • Vestibular ganglion (Scarpa’s ganglion) → balance

  • Spiral ganglion → hearing

  • Retina → vision

  • Olfactory epithelium → smell

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Cranial nerve ganglia – Most contain pseudounipolar sensory neurons (e.g., trigeminal ganglion), not typical bipolar neurons.

  • Cerebral cortex – Mainly contains multipolar neurons (e.g., pyramidal cells).

  • Cerebellar cortex – Contains mainly multipolar neurons (e.g., Purkinje cells).

High-yield points:

Neuron type Examples
Bipolar Vestibular ganglion, spiral ganglion, retina
Pseudounipolar Dorsal root ganglia, sensory cranial ganglia
Multipolar Motor neurons, cerebral cortex, Purkinje cells

Exam pearl:
Bipolar neuron = special sensory ganglia (vestibular & spiral ganglia).

Physiology-03.question: ৪৭) Neuroglia is non-excitable cell of CNS. Which of the following neuroglia is originated from Bone marrow?
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is microglia. Microglia are the only neuroglial cells of the CNS derived from bone marrow (mesodermal origin). They are the resident macrophages of the CNS and perform immune surveillance and phagocytosis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ependymocytes – Derived from neuroectoderm; line the ventricles and central canal, helping in CSF circulation.

  • Astrocytes – Derived from neuroectoderm; provide structural and metabolic support, maintain the blood–brain barrier.

  • Oligodendrocytes – Derived from neuroectoderm; responsible for myelination of CNS axons.

High-yield points:

Neuroglia Origin Function
Microglia Mesoderm / bone marrow (monocyte lineage) CNS macrophage
Astrocyte Neuroectoderm BBB support, repair
Oligodendrocyte Neuroectoderm CNS myelin formation
Ependymocyte Neuroectoderm CSF production/circulation

Exam pearl:
Microglia = macrophage of CNS = mesodermal origin.

Physiology-03.question: ৪৮) Which prevents fall of GFR?
৪৯) Secretion of K+ by the distal tubule will be decreased by -
Physiology-03.exp:
The correct answer is spironolactone administration. Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist that blocks aldosterone receptors in the distal nephron, resulting in:

  • ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption

  • ↓ K⁺ secretion

  • ↓ H⁺ secretion

Therefore, it is a potassium-sparing diuretic.

The other options increase distal K⁺ secretion:

  • High-K⁺ diet – Stimulates aldosterone secretion → ↑ K⁺ secretion by distal tubules.

  • Hyperaldosteronism – Increases ENaC activity and Na⁺ reabsorption → increased K⁺ secretion → hypokalaemia.

  • Thiazide diuretic administration – Increases Na⁺ delivery to distal nephron → promotes K⁺ secretion.

High-yield points:

Factors affecting distal K⁺ secretion:

↑ K⁺ secretion:

  • Aldosterone ↑

  • High K⁺ intake

  • Thiazide/loop diuretics

↓ K⁺ secretion:

  • Spironolactone

  • Amiloride

  • Triamterene
